title: 2.3.26 Rewrite the Traffic Light as a Switch
description: Rewrite an if/else-if chain that checks a traffic light color as an equivalent switch statement. Auto-graded.

steps.title: Read the given if/else-if chain
steps.instructions: The comment at the top of script.js shows the chain you're rewriting. It's already there for reference: don't delete it.

steps.title: Write the equivalent switch
steps.instructions: First create a variable called light set to "green", "yellow" or "red". Below the comment, write a switch on light with cases for 'green', 'yellow', and 'red', plus a default for anything else. Match the same messages as the original chain.

planChart.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[set light]
  B --> C{light is green}
  C -- yes --> D[/log Go/]
  C -- no --> E{light is yellow}
  E -- yes --> F[/log Slow down/]
  E -- no --> G{light is red}
  G -- yes --> H[/log Stop/]
  G -- no --> I[/log Broken light/]
  D --> J([End])
  F --> J
  H --> J
  I --> J

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your code
aiCheck.prompt: The student wrote JavaScript for the lab "2.3.26 Rewrite the Traffic Light as a Switch". The task they were given: The comment at the top of script.js shows the chain you're rewriting. It's already there for reference: don't delete it. You cannot run their code: read it and judge what it WOULD do. Judge each criterion by whether the idea is achieved, however the student wrote it. Different variable and function names, template strings, arrow functions, semicolons, spacing, quotes and order are all fine. Do not require any particular structure unless the criterion names one. Mark a criterion missing only when the idea is absent or the code does the opposite. Code inside a comment never runs. Write each note for THIS student's own code: in a not-met note, name the exact line or name in their code that causes the problem (quote at most a few words of it), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected code. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their code satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.
